explanation: In one of the [plural noun] that or who, the relative pronoun refers to the plural noun, so the verb in the clause is plural: several cats are unable to roar, and the snow leopard is one of them. Thus are is correct.
rationale: Singular verb with a plural antecedent: is treats that as referring to one animal, but that refers to cats, the group of animals that cannot roar.
Correct: that refers to the plural cats (several cats are unable to roar), so the plural verb are is needed in the relative clause.
Singular verb with a plural antecedent: has been does not agree with cats, the noun that the relative pronoun that refers to.
Singular verb with a plural antecedent: was does not agree with the plural cats and shifts to the past tense in a present-tense description.

stem: Of the forty applicants interviewed for the fellowship so far, Marisol is the only one who ____ fieldwork on three different continents.
explanation: When the antecedent is the only one, the relative clause refers to that single person, so its verb is singular. Marisol alone completed the fieldwork, so who has completed is correct; contrast one of the applicants who have.
rationale: Plural verb with a singular antecedent: have completed treats who as referring to applicants, but the only one limits the clause to Marisol alone.
Plural verb with a singular antecedent: were completing does not agree with the only one, the singular antecedent of who.
Plural verb with a singular antecedent: are completing cannot agree with the singular the only one, which who refers to.
Correct: who refers to the only one, a singular antecedent, so the singular verb has completed is right.

stem: The chief obstacle to restoring the old canal ____ the dozens of privately owned parcels along its banks, each of which would require a separate negotiation.
explanation: A linking verb agrees with its subject, not with the noun that follows the verb. The subject is the singular obstacle; parcels is the complement. So is is correct, even though the plural parcels comes right after the verb.
rationale: Correct: the subject is the singular obstacle, so the linking verb is agrees with it; the plural parcels is the complement, not the subject.
Plural verb with a singular subject: are agrees with the complement parcels, but the verb must agree with the subject obstacle.
Plural verb with a singular subject: have been cannot agree with the singular subject obstacle.
Plural verb with a singular subject: were treats the complement parcels as the subject, but the subject of the sentence is the singular obstacle.

stem: How the builders of the ancient monument transported forty-ton stones across nearly twenty miles of hilly terrain ____ one of the most debated questions in British archaeology.
explanation: A noun clause used as a subject is singular, no matter how many plural nouns it contains. The subject is the entire clause How the builders ... terrain, a single question, so the singular verb remains is correct.
rationale: Plural verb with a singular subject: remain agrees with stones or miles, but those nouns are inside the subject clause; the clause as a whole is singular.
Plural verb with a singular subject: have remained cannot agree with a noun clause subject, which is singular.
Correct: the noun clause how the builders transported the stones is a single idea and takes the singular verb remains.
Plural verb with a singular subject: are would require a plural subject, but the noun clause that begins with how is singular.

stem: Neither the museum's curator nor the two conservators who examined the painting under ultraviolet light ____ willing to say whether the signature was added later.
explanation: With neither...nor, the verb agrees with the nearer subject. The nearer subject is the plural conservators; the clause who examined the painting does not change that. The past-tense context calls for were.
rationale: Singular verb with a plural nearer subject: was agrees with curator, but the subject closer to the verb is the plural conservators.
Correct: the verb agrees with the nearer subject, the plural conservators, and the past-tense were matches examined and was added.
Singular verb with a plural nearer subject: has been does not agree with conservators, the subject nearest the verb.
Singular verb with a plural nearer subject: is cannot agree with the plural conservators and shifts to the present tense in a past-tense sentence.

stem: Roughly two-thirds of the seedlings raised in the greenhouse ____ transplanted to the hillside each spring, while the rest are kept for another year to strengthen their roots.
explanation: With a fraction or percentage, the verb agrees with the noun that follows of. Two-thirds of the seedlings refers to many individual plants, so the plural verb are is correct; two-thirds of the soil would take a singular verb.
rationale: Singular verb with a plural subject: is ignores the plural seedlings that determines agreement after a fraction.
Singular verb with a plural subject: has been does not agree with seedlings and does not fit the habitual each spring.
Singular verb with a plural subject: was does not agree with the plural seedlings and shifts to the past despite each spring and are kept.
Correct: after a fraction, the verb agrees with the noun in the of phrase; seedlings is plural, so are transplanted is right.

stem: Not only the marathon's race director but also the city's transit agency ____ responsible for rerouting buses around the course on race day, a task that takes months of planning.
explanation: With not only...but also, the verb agrees with the subject nearer to it, just as with either...or. The nearer subject is the singular transit agency, so is is correct.
rationale: Correct: with not only...but also, the verb agrees with the nearer subject, the singular transit agency, so is is right.
Plural verb with singular subjects: are treats not only...but also like and, but the verb agrees with the nearer subject, the singular transit agency.
Plural verb with a singular nearer subject: have been does not agree with transit agency, the subject nearest the verb.
Plural verb with a singular nearer subject: were does not agree with the singular transit agency and shifts the sentence into the past tense.

stem: One of the main reasons that the early iron bridges failed so often ____ the brittle rivets holding their girders together, which cracked easily in cold weather.
explanation: The subject is the singular pronoun one; reasons and bridges belong to the phrase and clause that follow it, and rivets is the complement after the verb. The verb agrees with the subject, so the singular past-tense was is correct.
rationale: Plural verb with a singular subject: were agrees with reasons, bridges, or rivets, but the subject of the sentence is the singular one.
Plural verb with a singular subject: have been does not agree with one, the true subject.
Correct: the subject is the singular one (of the main reasons), so was agrees with it despite the plural nouns nearby.
Plural verb with a singular subject: are does not agree with one and shifts to the present tense in a sentence about early bridges.

stem: Attached to the back of the portrait, hidden for more than a century beneath layers of brown paper, ____ two letters from the sitter to the painter.
explanation: When a sentence begins with a participial phrase and the verb precedes the subject, the verb must agree with the subject that follows. The subject is the plural two letters, so were is correct.
rationale: Singular verb with a plural subject: was agrees with portrait or paper, but the subject that follows the verb is the plural two letters.
Correct: the sentence is inverted, so the verb agrees with the plural subject two letters that follows it; were is right.
Singular verb with a plural subject: has been cannot agree with the plural two letters.
Singular verb with a plural subject: is does not agree with the plural subject two letters.

stem: Before the auction, every painting and every sculpture in the estate's collection ____ photographed, measured, and assigned a lot number by the appraiser's assistants.
explanation: When each or every comes before a compound subject, the subject is treated as singular, because the items are considered one at a time. Every painting and every sculpture therefore takes was, not were.
rationale: Correct: a compound subject introduced by every is singular, since each item is considered individually, so the singular past-tense was is right.
Plural verb with an every subject: were treats painting and sculpture as a plural pair, but every makes the compound subject singular.
Plural verb with an every subject: have been does not agree with the singular subject every painting and every sculpture.
Plural verb with an every subject: are does not agree with the singular subject introduced by every.

stem: In 1897, the Swedish engineer Salomon Andrée and two companions ____ to reach the North Pole by hydrogen balloon, a flight that ended on the pack ice after only three days.
explanation: A verb's tense must match the time established in the passage. The date 1897 and the past-tense verb ended place the events firmly in the past, so the simple past attempted is required.
rationale: Tense shift: the present-tense attempt clashes with the 1897 date and with the past-tense ended later in the sentence.
Correct: the simple past attempted matches the 1897 date and the past-tense ended.
Present progressive: are attempting describes an action happening now, but the flight took place in 1897 and has already ended.
Future tense: will attempt cannot describe an event that took place in 1897.

stem: Although the abacus was invented thousands of years ago, shopkeepers in some parts of the world still ____ it today to total purchases quickly and accurately.
explanation: Choose the tense that fits the time cues. The words still and today signal an action in the present, so the present-tense use is required even though the first clause describes the past.
rationale: Tense error: the past-tense used contradicts the cues still and today, which describe present practice.
Past perfect: had used describes an action completed before another past event, but the sentence is about what happens today.
Correct: the present-tense use matches the time cues still and today.
Future perfect: will have used places the action in the future, contradicting today.

stem: By the time the rescue team reached the stranded climbers, the storm ____ for nearly two days, and the group's supplies were almost gone.
explanation: The past perfect (had + past participle) shows that one past action was completed, or had been going on, before another past action. The storm was raging before the team reached the climbers, so had raged is correct.
rationale: Present perfect: has raged connects a past action to the present, but the sentence's reference point is the past-tense reached.
Present tense: rages does not fit a sentence anchored in the past by reached and were.
Future perfect: will have raged describes completion before a future point, but the rescue is in the past.
Correct: had raged (past perfect) shows the storm had been going on before the rescue team arrived, a past event.

stem: Since its founding in 2010, the neighborhood tool library ____ from a single shelf of donated hammers and drills to a collection of more than 3,000 items that members can borrow free of charge.
explanation: An action that began at a stated point in the past and continues to the present takes the present perfect (has or have + past participle). The phrase since its founding in 2010 spans past to present, so has grown is required.
rationale: Simple past: grew treats the growth as finished in the past, but since 2010 stretches the action to the present.
Correct: has grown (present perfect) fits an action that started in 2010 and continues now.
Past perfect: had grown requires a later past reference point, and none exists here.
Simple present: grows cannot describe a change that has unfolded since 2010.

stem: The Voyager 1 probe, launched in 1977 and now more than 15 billion miles from Earth, ____ to transmit faint signals that take nearly a full day to reach mission controllers.
explanation: Every sentence needs a main verb in a finite form. The subject The Voyager 1 probe is followed by a long descriptive phrase, and only continues supplies the finite verb; the -ing, to-, and having forms leave the sentence without one.
rationale: Correct: continues is a finite verb, giving the subject The Voyager 1 probe a complete predicate.
Fragment: the participle continuing cannot serve as a main verb, so the sentence has no predicate.
Fragment: the infinitive to continue is not a finite verb and leaves the sentence incomplete.
Fragment: having continued is a participial form, not a main verb, so the sentence is incomplete.

stem: When the archivist finally opened the water-stained trunk, she discovered a bundle of letters that had ____ untouched beneath a moth-eaten uniform for more than a century.
explanation: After the auxiliary had, a verb must be in its past participle form. The intransitive verb lie (to rest) has the forms lie, lay, lain, so had lain is correct. Laid is the participle of lay (to place something) and would need an object; lay is the past tense, not the participle.
rationale: Wrong verb: laid is the past participle of lay, meaning to place something, which requires an object; the letters were not placing anything.
Wrong form: lay is the simple past of lie; the auxiliary had must be followed by the past participle lain.
Wrong verb: lied is the participle of lie meaning to tell an untruth, which makes no sense here.
Correct: lain is the past participle of lie (to rest), the form required after had.

stem: After reviewing the draft, the independent auditor recommended that the financial report ____ revised to include the cost of the pension settlement before it was released to shareholders.
explanation: A that-clause following verbs such as recommend, demand, suggest, and insist takes the subjunctive: the base form of the verb, with no ending and no tense. The base form be is therefore correct; is, was, and will be are indicative forms.
rationale: Indicative: is is a present-tense form, but the clause after recommended that requires the subjunctive base form be.
Indicative: was is a past-tense form and does not express a recommendation about what should happen.
Correct: the base form be is the subjunctive required after recommended that.
Future indicative: will be states a prediction rather than a recommendation and cannot follow recommended that.

stem: The traveling exhibit of Inuit prints opened at the museum last spring and ____ more than 40,000 visitors before it closed in September.
explanation: Verbs joined by and in the same sentence should share a tense unless the meaning requires a change. Opened and closed are simple past, and the exhibit is already over, so the simple past attracted keeps the tense consistent.
rationale: Tense shift: the present-tense attracts does not match opened and closed, which describe a finished event.
Present perfect: has attracted implies the attracting may continue, but the exhibit closed in September.
Future: will attract cannot describe an exhibit that has already closed.
Correct: attracted matches the past-tense opened and closed and describes a completed event.

stem: ____ in 1889 as the entrance arch for that year's world's fair, the Eiffel Tower was intended to stand for only twenty years before being dismantled.
explanation: An introductory phrase that describes the subject must be a participle, not a finite verb, and its voice must fit the subject. The tower was built by others, so the past participle Built (passive) is correct; Building and Having built are active and would mean the tower did the building, while Was built creates a clause with no subject.
rationale: Correct: the past participle Built forms a passive modifier describing the Eiffel Tower.
Wrong voice: the present participle Building would mean the tower was doing the building.
Finite verb without a subject: Was built in 1889 cannot serve as an introductory modifier.
Wrong voice: Having built is active and would mean the tower had built something itself.

stem: When the excavation team broke the seal on the tomb in 1922, they realized that ancient robbers ____ the burial chamber at least twice and had carried off most of the smaller gold objects.
explanation: Use the past perfect (had + past participle) for an action completed before another past action. The robbers' entries happened before the team broke the seal, and the parallel verb had carried off confirms the past perfect.
rationale: Present perfect: have already entered links the robbery to the present, but the reference point is the past-tense broke.
Present tense: already enter cannot describe actions completed before a 1922 event.
Correct: had already entered (past perfect) shows the robberies occurred before the team broke the seal, and it matches had carried off.
Future perfect: will already have entered places the robbery in the future, contradicting the 1922 date.

stem: The physicist Marie Curie, who remains the only person to have won Nobel Prizes in two different sciences, ____ the term radioactivity to describe the rays she observed coming from uranium.
explanation: A sentence must have a main verb in a finite form. The subject Marie Curie is separated from its verb by a who clause, and only coined is a finite verb; the -ing, having, and to forms would leave the sentence without a predicate.
rationale: Fragment: coining is a participle and cannot act as the main verb for the subject Marie Curie.
Correct: coined is a finite past-tense verb that completes the sentence.
Fragment: having coined is a participial phrase, not a main verb.
Fragment: the infinitive to coin cannot serve as the sentence's main verb.

stem: If the Moon ____ only half as far from Earth as it is now, ocean tides would be roughly eight times stronger, flooding low-lying coastlines twice each day.
explanation: A condition that is contrary to fact takes the subjunctive were in the if-clause, paired with would in the main clause. The Moon is not half as far away, so were is correct; was is the indicative past, and would and will do not belong in the if-clause.
rationale: Indicative: was states a past fact, but the sentence describes a hypothetical situation, which requires the subjunctive were.
Future: will be does not belong in a hypothetical if-clause paired with would be.
Conditional in the if-clause: would be belongs in the main clause, not in the if-clause.
Correct: the subjunctive were expresses a condition contrary to fact.

stem: The zoning board, ____ the proposal for a rooftop apiary at three separate meetings, finally approved it on the condition that the hives be inspected twice a year.
explanation: A phrase set off by commas between the subject and its main verb must be a participle, not a finite verb. Having debated is a perfect participle that shows the debating came before the approval; debated, debates, and had debated would each add a second finite verb and break the sentence.
rationale: Correct: the perfect participle having debated modifies the zoning board and shows the debate preceded the approval.
Broken structure: debated after the comma either adds a second finite verb with no connector or, read as a participle, wrongly means the board itself was debated.
Second finite verb: debates cannot sit inside the commas as a modifier of the board.
Second finite verb: had debated turns the modifier into a clause with no conjunction, breaking the sentence.

stem: During the 1883 eruption of Krakatoa, the sound of the volcano's final explosion ____ heard nearly 3,000 miles away, on the island of Rodrigues in the Indian Ocean.
explanation: Match the verb to the time cue. The date 1883 fixes the event in the completed past, so the simple past was is correct; is and has been reach into the present, and had been requires a later past event to precede.
rationale: Present tense: is contradicts the 1883 date.
Present perfect: has been links the sound to the present, but the eruption is a completed past event.
Correct: was fits an event that occurred in 1883.
Past perfect: had been needs another past event that came afterward, and none is mentioned.

stem: By the time the lifeguards spotted him from the pier, the boy ____ nearly a quarter mile beyond the line of buoys and was struggling against the outgoing tide.
explanation: The past perfect is formed with had plus the past participle. The participle of swim is swum (swim, swam, swum), so had swum is correct; swam is the simple past and cannot follow had, and swum alone leaves the clause without a finite verb.
rationale: Wrong participle: swam is the simple past form; after had, the participle swum is required.
Correct: had swum uses the proper past participle and shows the swimming happened before the lifeguards spotted him.
Wrong participle and tense: has swam pairs an auxiliary with the wrong form and shifts to the present.
No finite verb: swum by itself cannot serve as the verb of the clause.

stem: In the opening chapter of the novel, the narrator describes the fishing village in painstaking detail and ____ the reader to notice how every household depends on the tides.
explanation: Verbs describing what happens in a literary work are written in the present tense, and verbs joined by and should stay in the same tense. Describes is present, so invites keeps the compound predicate consistent.
rationale: Tense shift: invited is past tense, but it is joined by and to the present-tense describes.
Past perfect: had invited implies an action completed before another past action, but the sentence is in the literary present.
Future: will invite does not match the present-tense describes.
Correct: invites matches describes, keeping both verbs in the present tense used to discuss literature.

stem: Had the levee along the river's eastern bank been reinforced before last spring's storm, the flooding that followed ____ far less severe, according to the engineers' report.
explanation: An inverted conditional (Had the levee been reinforced) expresses a past condition contrary to fact, and its main clause takes would have + past participle. The flooding already happened, so would have been is correct.
rationale: Correct: would have been is the result form for a past counterfactual condition.
Wrong time: would be describes a present or future result, but the flooding followed last spring's storm.
Future perfect: will have been treats the flooding as still to come.
Indicative: was states the flooding as fact, ignoring the hypothetical condition set up by Had ... been reinforced.

stem: After inspectors found cracks in the new gymnasium's foundation, the school board demanded that the contractor ____ the damage at no additional cost to the district.
explanation: After demand that, the verb in the that-clause takes the subjunctive base form, with no -s or -ed ending. Repair is that base form; repairs and repaired are indicative, and would repair states a prediction rather than a demand.
rationale: Indicative: repairs adds the present-tense -s, but a clause after demanded that requires the base form.
Indicative past: repaired reports a completed action rather than expressing what was demanded.
Correct: the base form repair is the subjunctive required after demanded that.
Conditional: would repair does not belong in a subjunctive clause following demanded that.

stem: Each morning the baker ____ the wood-fired ovens at four o'clock, shapes the sourdough loaves by five, and unlocks the shop door promptly at seven.
explanation: Verbs in a series should share the same tense unless the meaning calls for a change. Shapes and unlocks are simple present, describing a daily routine, so lights is required.
rationale: Tense shift: the past-tense lit does not match the present-tense shapes and unlocks.
Correct: lights matches shapes and unlocks and fits the routine signaled by each morning.
Past perfect: had lit describes a completed past action, inconsistent with the present-tense series.
Past progressive: was lighting clashes with the present-tense verbs that follow.

stem: The Roman aqueduct at Segovia, ____ without mortar from roughly 20,000 granite blocks, still carried water into the twentieth century.
explanation: A descriptive phrase set off by commas between a subject and its verb must be a participle. The past participle built works as a passive modifier of aqueduct; was built and has been built are finite verbs that would create a second, unconnected clause, and building would wrongly mean the aqueduct did the building.
rationale: Correct: the past participle built forms a passive phrase describing the aqueduct.
Second finite verb: was built inside the commas creates a clause with no conjunction, breaking the sentence.
Wrong voice: the present participle building would mean the aqueduct was constructing something.
Second finite verb: has been built cannot serve as a modifier between the subject and its verb carried.

stem: By the time the ship's carpenter finished patching the hull, the tide ____ so far that the vessel sat on bare mud, and the crew had no choice but to wait for morning.
explanation: When one past action was completed before another past action, the earlier action takes the past perfect. The tide went out before the carpenter finished, so had receded is required; the other choices shift the tide's movement into the present or future.
rationale: Present tense: recedes does not fit a narrative anchored in the past by finished and sat.
Present perfect: has receded connects to the present, but the reference point is the past-tense finished.
Future perfect: will have receded describes completion before a future moment, not before a past one.
Correct: had receded (past perfect) shows the tide had gone out before the carpenter finished.

stem: Biologists ____ the same colony of leafcutter ants for six years now, yet they still cannot explain why the workers abandon a perfectly healthy fungus garden every third summer.
explanation: An action that began in the past and continues into the present takes the present perfect. The phrase for six years now and the present-tense still cannot explain show the monitoring is ongoing, so have monitored is correct.
rationale: Simple past: monitored presents the study as finished, but for six years now and still cannot explain show it continues.
Past perfect: had monitored needs a later past event as a reference point; the sentence is anchored in the present.
Correct: have monitored (present perfect) describes an action that began six years ago and is still going on.
Simple present: monitor cannot express a duration that reaches from six years ago to now.

stem: The freighter, which struck the reef shortly after midnight while carrying a full load of iron ore, ____ within minutes, giving the crew barely enough time to launch the lifeboats.
explanation: The simple past of sink is sank; sunk is the past participle and can be used only with an auxiliary such as had. The sentence needs a finite past-tense verb to match struck, so sank is correct.
rationale: Participle without an auxiliary: sunk cannot serve as the main verb by itself.
Wrong form: sank is the simple past, not the participle needed after has, and the present perfect clashes with struck.
Fragment: the participle sinking leaves the subject the freighter without a main verb.
Correct: sank is the simple past form and matches the past-tense struck.

stem: If Emily Dickinson ____ alive today, she might be astonished to learn that nearly 1,800 of her poems have been published, since fewer than a dozen appeared in print during her lifetime.
explanation: A hypothetical condition that is contrary to fact takes the subjunctive were. Dickinson is not alive today, so were is required; was is the indicative past, is treats the condition as real, and had been shifts the condition into the past despite the word today.
rationale: Correct: the subjunctive were expresses a condition contrary to fact.
Indicative: was reports a past fact rather than expressing a hypothetical, so it does not fit a contrary-to-fact if-clause.
Real condition: is treats her being alive as a genuine possibility, which contradicts the sentence's meaning.
Wrong time: had been places the condition in the past, clashing with today and might be.

stem: The unusual mix of fossils on the island suggests that the flightless bird ____ in isolation for millions of years, long after its mainland relatives had died out.
explanation: The subjunctive follows suggest only when it means propose or recommend. Here suggests means indicates, so the that-clause reports a finding and takes an ordinary indicative verb; the past-tense evolved fits the past frame set by had died out.
rationale: Misapplied subjunctive: the base form evolve would be needed only if suggests meant recommended, but here it means indicates.
Correct: evolved is an indicative past-tense verb, which is appropriate because suggests here means indicates rather than recommends.
Subjunctive form: be evolving treats the clause as a recommendation rather than a statement of what the evidence shows.
Hypothetical form: were to evolve describes an imagined condition, not evidence about what actually happened.

stem: ____ by the glare of the stadium's floodlights, thousands of migrating warblers circled the structure for hours instead of continuing south, a phenomenon researchers have documented in several cities.
explanation: An introductory participial phrase must match its subject in voice. The warblers were affected by the glare, so the passive past participle Disoriented is correct; Disorienting and Having disoriented would mean the birds confused something else, and Were disoriented is a finite verb with no subject.
rationale: Wrong voice: the present participle Disorienting would mean the warblers were causing confusion.
Wrong voice: Having disoriented is active and would mean the birds had confused the floodlights.
Correct: the past participle Disoriented shows the birds were confused by the lights.
Finite verb without a subject: Were disoriented cannot begin a modifying phrase.

stem: By the end of this decade, the survey telescope ____ more than a million wide-field images of the night sky, enough data to catalog billions of previously unrecorded objects.
explanation: The future perfect (will have + past participle) describes an action that will be complete by a stated future time. The phrase by the end of this decade points to the future, so will have collected is required.
rationale: Correct: will have collected shows the collecting will be finished by a future point, the end of this decade.
Present perfect: has collected describes what is already done, but the sentence looks ahead to the end of the decade.
Past perfect: had collected refers to completion before a past moment, not a future one.
Simple past: collected describes a finished past action and contradicts the future time cue.

stem: While the orchestra ____ the final movement of the symphony, a transformer failure plunged the concert hall into darkness, and the musicians finished the piece from memory.
explanation: The past progressive (was + -ing form) describes an action that was in progress when another past action interrupted it. The performance was under way when the power failed, so was performing is correct.
rationale: Present tense: performs clashes with the past-tense plunged and finished.
Present perfect: has performed links the action to the present, but the event is narrated in the past.
Past perfect: had performed would mean the movement was already over, contradicting while and finished the piece from memory.
Correct: was performing shows the performance was in progress when the failure interrupted it.

stem: The university library ____ the poet's handwritten notebooks in 1998, and they have been available to researchers in the rare books reading room ever since.
explanation: A completed action at a specific past time takes the simple past. The date 1998 fixes the acquisition in the past, so acquired is correct; the present perfect has acquired cannot be used with a specific past date, and had acquired needs a later past reference point.
rationale: Present perfect with a specific date: has acquired cannot combine with in 1998.
Present tense: acquires does not fit an event dated 1998.
Past perfect: had acquired requires another past event that followed it, and none is given.
Correct: acquired is the simple past appropriate for an action completed in 1998.

stem: Many longtime residents wish that the old opera house on Front Street ____ still standing, but the building was razed in 1971 to make room for a parking garage.
explanation: A wish about a situation that is contrary to fact takes the subjunctive were. The opera house was razed, so its still standing is imagined, not real; is, will be, and has been are indicative forms that treat the wish as a fact or a prediction.
rationale: Indicative: is treats the building's standing as a present fact, but the sentence says it was razed.
Correct: the subjunctive were expresses a wish contrary to fact.
Future: will be does not follow wish for a present contrary-to-fact situation; the building is already gone.
Present perfect: has been states a fact about the past and cannot express an unreal wish.

stem: By noon on the third day of rain, the creek behind the schoolhouse ____ nearly two feet above its banks, and the road to town was impassable.
explanation: The past perfect requires had plus the past participle. Rise is intransitive (it takes no object) and has the forms rise, rose, risen, so had risen is correct. Rose is the simple past, not the participle, and raised belongs to the transitive verb raise, which requires an object.
rationale: Correct: had risen uses the past participle risen of the intransitive verb rise.
Wrong form: rose is the simple past; after had, the participle risen is required.
Wrong form and tense: rose is not a participle, and the present perfect clashes with the past-tense was.
Wrong verb: raised is a form of raise, which must take an object; the creek did not raise anything.

stem: When the new radio telescope array becomes fully operational next year, astronomers ____ able to map the hydrogen clouds between galaxies in unprecedented detail.
explanation: The time cue next year places the action in the future. In a sentence about a future event, the when-clause uses the present tense (becomes) and the main clause uses will, so will be is correct.
rationale: Past tense: were contradicts the cue next year.
Past perfect: had been describes something completed before a past event, not a future ability.
Present perfect: have been links to the present, but the ability will begin next year.
Correct: will be matches the future time cue next year and the present-tense becomes in the when-clause.

stem: The Great Fire of London, ____ in a bakery on Pudding Lane in the early hours of September 2, 1666, destroyed more than 13,000 houses in four days.
explanation: A phrase between commas that describes the subject must be a participle, not a finite verb. Beginning is a participle that modifies The Great Fire of London; began, had begun, and begins are finite verbs that would give the sentence two main verbs with nothing joining them.
rationale: Second finite verb: began inside the commas creates a clause that collides with the main verb destroyed.
Correct: the participle beginning forms a modifying phrase describing the fire.
Second finite verb: had begun cannot function as a modifier set off by commas.
Second finite verb and tense shift: begins is a present-tense main verb, not a modifier.

stem: If the technicians ____ the tissue samples at the proper temperature, the results would not have been contaminated; instead, a malfunctioning freezer ruined the entire batch overnight.
explanation: A past condition contrary to fact takes the past perfect (had + past participle) in the if-clause, with would have in the main clause. The freezer malfunctioned, so the samples were not stored properly; had stored is required.
rationale: Wrong form: the simple past stored treats the condition as open, but the sentence makes clear it did not happen; a past counterfactual needs had stored.
Would in the if-clause: would have stored belongs in the result clause, not the condition.
Correct: had stored (past perfect) expresses a past condition that did not occur, matching would not have been contaminated.
Present perfect: have stored ties the condition to the present, but the contamination happened in the past.

stem: During the 1912 negotiations, the union's representatives proposed that every mill worker ____ given a written contract stating both the hourly wage and the maximum length of a shift.
explanation: After propose that, the verb in the that-clause takes the subjunctive base form. Be is that base form; was, is, and would be are indicative or conditional forms that report or predict rather than express what the union proposed.
rationale: Correct: the base form be is the subjunctive required after proposed that.
Indicative past: was reports a fact rather than stating what the union proposed.
Indicative present: is does not fit a proposal about what should happen.
Conditional: would be expresses a prediction, not the subjunctive proposal required here.

stem: The steel plant once employed more than 4,000 people; today it ____ fewer than 300, most of whom operate the automated rolling mill from a control room.
explanation: The tense must follow the time cues. The first clause, marked by once, is past, but today signals the present, so employs is correct for the second clause, matching the present-tense operate.
rationale: Tense error: employed is past, but today calls for the present tense.
Past perfect: had employed describes an earlier past action, contradicting today.
Correct: employs matches the cue today and the present-tense operate.
Future: will employ does not fit the cue today.

stem: The museum docent, ____ that the seventh-grade group had lost interest in the pottery collection, skipped ahead to the hall of medieval armor.
explanation: A phrase between commas that describes the subject must be a participle. The present participle sensing modifies docent and explains why she skipped ahead; sensed, senses, and had sensed are finite verbs that would give the sentence two main verbs joined by nothing.
rationale: Second finite verb: sensed inside the commas leaves the docent with two main verbs and no conjunction.
Second finite verb: senses is a present-tense main verb, not a modifier, and it clashes with skipped.
Correct: the participle sensing forms a modifying phrase describing the docent.
Second finite verb: had sensed creates an unconnected clause inside the commas.

stem: If the transcontinental telegraph had not been completed in 1861, news of President Lincoln's assassination four years later ____ weeks rather than hours to reach California.
explanation: When the if-clause uses the past perfect to describe a past condition contrary to fact, the main clause uses would have + past participle. The news traveled in 1865, so would have taken is the correct result form.
rationale: Wrong time: would take describes a present or future result, but the event happened in 1865.
Correct: would have taken is the result form matching the past counterfactual condition had not been completed.
Future perfect: will have taken treats the 1865 event as still to come.
Indicative past perfect: had taken states the delay as a fact, ignoring the hypothetical condition.

stem: By the time the last guests found their seats in the crowded auditorium, the graduation ceremony ____, and the principal was already midway through her welcoming remarks.
explanation: The past perfect uses had plus the past participle; the participle of begin is begun (begin, began, begun). Had begun is correct; began is the simple past and cannot follow had, and begun alone leaves the clause without a finite verb.
rationale: Wrong form and tense: began is not a participle, and has shifts to the present in a past narrative.
Wrong participle: began is the simple past; after had, begun is required.
Correct: had begun uses the proper participle and shows the ceremony started before the guests were seated.
No finite verb: begun by itself cannot be the verb of the clause.

stem: As the bell ____ to signal the end of the final period, the students in the chemistry lab hurried to rinse their glassware and record their last measurements.
explanation: The simple past of ring is rang; rung is the past participle and needs an auxiliary. The as-clause describes an action happening at the same time as the past-tense hurried, so the simple past rang is correct.
rationale: Correct: rang is the simple past, matching hurried and describing a simultaneous action.
Participle without an auxiliary: rung cannot act as the finite verb of the as-clause.
Present tense: rings clashes with the past-tense hurried.
Past perfect: had rung would mean the bell had already finished ringing, but as signals that the two actions occurred at the same time.
